reception.text: About 1,300 men and boys, most of them mounted and many armed, rushed across the line at noon on June 17, and the New-York Tribune put the land run on its front page.
The San Francisco Call reported sooners, a flood of applications, disappointed applicants and contests, and warned of bloodshed.
The Call also reported that long-resident settlers on the reservation were being filed on by newcomers, because the opening law gave them no protection.
The phrase "Fort Hall Reservation" appears on 149 digitized newspaper pages from May through July 1902, in at least thirteen states, though few papers reprinted the proclamation's text.

political_impact.text: The ceded lands opened on schedule on June 17, 1902, and the Pocatello lands were offered for sale on July 17, with no postponement or litigation.
political_impact.source: Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, 1902

political_impact.text: In the opening fortnight the Blackfoot land office recorded 126 sales under the 1900 act, on 17,539.91 acres, more than in the whole following year (106 sales on 6,668.56 acres).
political_impact.source: Report of the Commissioner of the General Land Office, 1902, p. 551; 1903, p. 225

political_impact.text: The Pocatello auction drew little interest, and the wire report predicted few tracts would sell.

After two white men were found murdered near new mining claims, some people in Pocatello asked the governor for troops; the Fort Hall agent reported no excitement among the Indians and no need for troops.
political_impact.source: A. F. Caldwell, Annual Report of the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, 1902, pp. 181–182

legacy.text: The general allotment of the diminished reservation came only in 1911, and Fort Hall remains among the least fractionated of allotted reservations, with most land in tribal ownership or trust.

The tribes' claim that the 1898 cession was made for an unconscionable price, Docket 326-E, was settled in 1968 within a $15,700,000 judgment covering seven Fort Hall dockets, with no part assigned to this cession.

today.name: Lava Hot Springs (state resort)
today.note: Held back from settlement by the proclamation and granted to Idaho by a separate act of June 13, 1902; run by the Lava Hot Springs Foundation within the Idaho Department of Parks and Recreation.

later_actions.text: Congress granted the Lava Hot Springs tract, reserved in the proclamation, to Idaho for public use.
Congress provided for the general allotment of the diminished Fort Hall Reservation.
The Indian Claims Commission entered a consolidated $15,700,000 settlement of seven Fort Hall dockets, including the claim over the 1898 cession.

uncertain: Whether minutes of the 1896–98 Fort Hall councils survive is not known.
How many people filed homestead claims on the ceded lands is not known; the land office tables do not separate them.
The acreage figures 416,060 and 406,864 have not been traced to a measured source; the commissioners estimated about 416,000 acres.
